params.question: A 4-year-old presents with fever, cough, and crackles in the right lower zone. She is feeding well, her oxygen saturation is 97%, and this is her first episode. What is the most appropriate imaging decision?

answers.text: Order a chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis of pneumonia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In uncomplicated pneumonia with no hypoxia, no severity signs, and a clear clinical picture, a chest X-ray does not change management and adds unnecessary radiation.

answers.text: Treat clinically and image only if she fails to improve in 48–72 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The WHO and most guidelines state that routine radiography is not required for uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia. If she worsens or fails to improve in 48–72 hours, imaging is then justified to look for complications.

answers.text: Request frontal and lateral chest X-ray views for completeness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A routine lateral view adds radiation dose without significant diagnostic benefit in paediatric pneumonia. Moreover, imaging is not indicated in this uncomplicated case.

answers.text: Perform a CT thorax to rule out underlying complications

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT carries a far higher radiation dose and is reserved for confirmed complications such as necrotising pneumonia or lung abscess. It is never a first-line investigation for uncomplicated pneumonia.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the WHO position: routine radiography is not required for uncomplicated paediatric pneumonia. Children are especially radiosensitive, so image only when the result will change management.
Well done. In uncomplicated pneumonia — no hypoxia, feeding well, first episode — the diagnosis is clinical and imaging is deferred unless the child fails to improve.

interactions.label: A child with pneumonia has a dull lung base and the chest X-ray shows a pleural

params.question: A child with pneumonia has a dull lung base and the chest X-ray shows a pleural opacity. Which investigation should be performed next to guide management?

answers.text: CT thorax to determine the density and extent of the fluid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT thorax is reserved for parenchymal complications such as necrotising pneumonia or abscess. For pleural fluid, ultrasound answers the clinical question without ionising radiation.

answers.text: Repeat chest X-ray with a lateral view to confirm the opacity is pleural

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A lateral view adds radiation dose without characterising the fluid. It cannot distinguish simple effusion from empyema.

answers.text: Chest ultrasound to characterise the fluid and distinguish simple effusion from empyema

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Ultrasound carries no ionising radiation, is more sensitive than plain film for small effusions, and distinguishes free-flowing simple effusion from septated empyema — directly guiding drainage decisions.

answers.text: Diagnostic thoracentesis to obtain a sample of the fluid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Thoracentesis is an invasive procedure. Ultrasound should first characterise the collection non-invasively and, if drainage is needed, guide the procedure site.

overallFeedback.feedback: When a chest X-ray shows a pleural opacity, the next step is chest ultrasound — it carries no ionising radiation and can distinguish simple effusion from septated empyema, guiding whether drainage is needed.
Exactly right. The clinical pearl is: when there is fluid, reach for the probe, not the scanner. Ultrasound characterises pleural collections without ionising radiation.

params.question: A 2-year-old choked on a peanut 6 hours ago. The expiratory chest X-ray shows the left lung remains hyperinflated while the right lung deflates normally, and the mediastinum has shifted to the right. What mechanism explains these findings?

answers.text: Complete obstruction of the left main bronchus causing lobar collapse

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complete obstruction causes collapse of the affected lung, not hyperinflation. With collapse, the mediastinum shifts toward the affected side, not away from it.

answers.text: Partial obstruction of the left main bronchus acting as a ball-valve

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The peanut causes partial obstruction: air enters past the foreign body on inspiration but is trapped on expiration. This produces unilateral hyperinflation, and the mediastinum shifts away from the hyperinflated side.

answers.text: Complete obstruction of the right main bronchus with compensatory left hyperinflation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The right lung is deflating normally on expiration, which is the expected behaviour. The pathology is on the left side, where air is being trapped.
Tension pneumothorax shows absent lung markings with air in the pleural space, not hyperinflation of an aerated lung. The clinical history of choking points to foreign body obstruction.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the two directions: partial obstruction traps air (hyperinflation, mediastinum shifts AWAY); complete obstruction causes collapse (mediastinum shifts TOWARD). A peanut causing hyperinflation is a ball-valve — partial obstruction.
Well analysed. Partial bronchial obstruction acts as a ball-valve — air enters but cannot escape — producing hyperinflation with mediastinal shift away from the obstructed side.

params.question: A normal renal ultrasound reliably excludes vesicoureteric reflux in a child who has had a febrile urinary tract infection.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Ultrasound shows structure, not function. A normal renal ultrasound does not exclude vesicoureteric reflux, because reflux occurs during voiding and is invisible on a static scan. The MCUG, which images the bladder during voiding, is needed to diagnose and grade reflux.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Ultrasound reveals structural anatomy — hydronephrosis, cortical thinning, size asymmetry — but it cannot detect the backward flow of urine during voiding. A micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) is the specific investigation needed to diagnose and grade vesicoureteric reflux.

interactions.label: Which statement correctly links a paediatric condition to its definitive investi

params.question: Which statement correctly links a paediatric condition to its definitive investigation or management decision?

answers.text: Chest infection — CT thorax is the first-line imaging investigation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The chest X-ray, not CT, is the first-line investigation for chest infection. CT is reserved for complications such as necrotising pneumonia or lung abscess.

answers.text: Foreign body aspiration — a normal chest X-ray reliably excludes the diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A normal CXR is the most common finding in early aspiration. Most inhaled objects in children are organic and radiolucent. When clinical suspicion is strong, bronchoscopy is indicated regardless of the film.

answers.text: Foreign body aspiration — rigid bronchoscopy is indicated when the choking history is convincing, even with a normal chest X-ray

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic. A convincing choking history is itself an indication for bronchoscopy, because most inhaled objects in children are radiolucent and a normal CXR never excludes the diagnosis.

answers.text: Urinary tract infection — the DMSA scan diagnoses and grades vesicoureteric reflux

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The DMSA scan detects cortical damage and scarring, not reflux. Vesicoureteric reflux is diagnosed and graded by the micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG).

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the links: CXR (not CT) is first-line for chest infection; bronchoscopy (not CXR) is definitive for foreign body aspiration; MCUG diagnoses reflux while DMSA detects cortical scarring in UTI.

Well done. Across all three conditions, the key principle is to match the right investigation to the clinical question — and to act when clinical suspicion is strong, even if initial imaging appears normal.
